title: The Remainder Theorem
overview: Dividing polynomials works just like long division with numbers — and it has a powerful shortcut. In this section you will divide a polynomial by a binomial, write the answer in quotient form with its restriction, and use the **remainder theorem** to find a remainder instantly by substitution. You will use these tools to solve for unknown coefficients and to find the dimensions of objects from their volume.
objectives: Divide a polynomial by a binomial of the form $x - b$ or $ax - b$ using long division.
Write the result of a division in quotient form, state its restriction, and write the division statement.
Explain why the remainder theorem works.
Use the remainder theorem to find a remainder without dividing.
Solve for unknown coefficients using given remainders.
Solve problems, such as finding dimensions from a volume, using division.

lessons.title: Dividing polynomials: the big idea
lessons.body:
You already know how to divide whole numbers. When you divide $579$ by $8$ you get $72$ with a remainder of $3$, and you can **check** the answer by multiplying back:

$$579 = 8 \times 72 + 3$$

Polynomials work in exactly the same way. When a polynomial $P(x)$ (the **dividend**) is divided by a binomial $x - b$ (the **divisor**), you get a **quotient** $Q(x)$ and a **remainder** $R$:

$$P(x) = (x - b)\,Q(x) + R$$

This is called the **division statement**. You can also write the result in **quotient form**:

$$\frac{P(x)}{x - b} = Q(x) + \frac{R}{x - b}, \qquad x \neq b$$

| Whole numbers | Polynomials |
|---|---|
| dividend $579$ | dividend $P(x)$ |
| divisor $8$ | divisor $x - b$ |
| quotient $72$ | quotient $Q(x)$ |
| remainder $3$ | remainder $R$ |
| check: $8 \times 72 + 3 = 579$ | check: $(x-b)Q(x) + R = P(x)$ |

**Why the restriction $x \neq b$?** In quotient form you are dividing by $x - b$. If $x = b$, the divisor is $0$, and division by zero is undefined. So every time you write a quotient form you must state the **restriction** on $x$.

> **Degree check:** dividing a degree-$n$ polynomial by a linear binomial always gives a quotient of degree $n-1$, and the remainder is a constant (degree $0$).

lessons.title: Long division, one step at a time
lessons.body:
Long division of polynomials repeats the same four moves: **Divide → Multiply → Subtract → Bring down**. Always write both polynomials in **descending order of degree** first.

**Example:** divide $2x^3 - 3x^2 + 4x - 7$ by $x - 2$.

| Step | What you do | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Divide | $2x^3 \div x$ | $2x^2$ (first term of the quotient) |
| 2. Multiply | $2x^2(x - 2)$ | $2x^3 - 4x^2$ |
| 3. Subtract | $(2x^3 - 3x^2) - (2x^3 - 4x^2)$ | $x^2$, then bring down $+4x$: $\;x^2 + 4x$ |
| 4. Divide | $x^2 \div x$ | $+x$ |
| 5. Multiply | $x(x - 2)$ | $x^2 - 2x$ |
| 6. Subtract | $(x^2 + 4x) - (x^2 - 2x)$ | $6x$, then bring down $-7$: $\;6x - 7$ |
| 7. Divide | $6x \div x$ | $+6$ |
| 8. Multiply | $6(x - 2)$ | $6x - 12$ |
| 9. Subtract | $(6x - 7) - (6x - 12)$ | $5$ ← the **remainder** |

So the quotient is $2x^2 + x + 6$ and the remainder is $5$:

$$\frac{2x^3 - 3x^2 + 4x - 7}{x - 2} = 2x^2 + x + 6 + \frac{5}{x - 2}, \quad x \neq 2$$

**Check:** $(x - 2)(2x^2 + x + 6) + 5 = 2x^3 + x^2 + 6x - 4x^2 - 2x - 12 + 5 = 2x^3 - 3x^2 + 4x - 7$ ✓

### Placeholders for missing terms
If a power of $x$ is missing, insert it with a coefficient of $0$ **before** you divide. For example, write $x^3 - 7x + 6$ as $x^3 + 0x^2 - 7x + 6$. The placeholder keeps like terms lined up in columns, so you never subtract an $x$ term from an $x^2$ term by mistake.

> **Tip:** subtracting is where most errors happen. Change the sign of every term in the line you are subtracting, then add.

lessons.title: Dividing by a binomial of the form ax − b
lessons.body:
The same process works when the divisor's leading coefficient is not $1$, such as $2x - 1$ or $3x + 2$. The only difference is that each "divide" step now divides by $ax$.

**Example:** divide $6x^3 + 5x^2 - 2x + 4$ by $2x - 1$.

| Step | Work | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Divide | $6x^3 \div 2x$ | $3x^2$ |
| Multiply, subtract | $(6x^3 + 5x^2) - (6x^3 - 3x^2)$ | $8x^2$; bring down: $8x^2 - 2x$ |
| Divide | $8x^2 \div 2x$ | $+4x$ |
| Multiply, subtract | $(8x^2 - 2x) - (8x^2 - 4x)$ | $2x$; bring down: $2x + 4$ |
| Divide | $2x \div 2x$ | $+1$ |
| Multiply, subtract | $(2x + 4) - (2x - 1)$ | $5$ |

$$\frac{6x^3 + 5x^2 - 2x + 4}{2x - 1} = 3x^2 + 4x + 1 + \frac{5}{2x - 1}, \quad x \neq \tfrac{1}{2}$$

The restriction comes from setting the divisor equal to zero: $2x - 1 = 0 \Rightarrow x = \tfrac12$.

lessons.title: The remainder theorem: the remainder without dividing
lessons.body:
Look again at the division statement $P(x) = (x - b)Q(x) + R$. It is true for **every** value of $x$, so substitute $x = b$:

$$P(b) = (b - b)\,Q(b) + R = 0 \cdot Q(b) + R = R$$

That gives the **remainder theorem**:

> When a polynomial $P(x)$ is divided by $x - b$, the remainder is $P(b)$.
> When $P(x)$ is divided by $ax - b$, the remainder is $P\!\left(\tfrac{b}{a}\right)$.

**Finding the right value to substitute.** Set the divisor equal to zero and solve:

| Divisor | Solve divisor $= 0$ | Remainder |
|---|---|---|
| $x - 3$ | $x = 3$ | $P(3)$ |
| $x + 4$ | $x = -4$ | $P(-4)$ |
| $2x - 1$ | $x = \tfrac12$ | $P\!\left(\tfrac12\right)$ |
| $3x + 2$ | $x = -\tfrac23$ | $P\!\left(-\tfrac23\right)$ |

**Example:** the remainder when $P(x) = 2x^3 - 3x^2 + 4x - 7$ is divided by $x - 2$ is
$P(2) = 2(8) - 3(4) + 4(2) - 7 = 16 - 12 + 8 - 7 = 5$, which matches the long division.

**Graph connection.** $P(b) = R$ means the point $(b, R)$ is on the graph of $y = P(x)$. The remainder is simply the height of the graph at $x = b$.

```plot
title: The remainder when P(x) = 2x³ − 3x² + 4x − 7 is divided by x − 2 is P(2) = 5
f: 2*x^3 - 3*x^2 + 4*x - 7 | label=y = P(x)
domain: -1.5, 3
range: -25, 25
ticks: 0.5, 5
points: (2, 5)
```

> The remainder theorem gives the **remainder only**. If you also need the quotient, you still have to divide.

lessons.title: Using the remainder theorem to find unknown coefficients
lessons.body:
If you know the remainder, the remainder theorem gives you an **equation** you can solve.

**One unknown.** Find $k$ if $x^3 + kx^2 - 4x + 5$ leaves a remainder of $8$ when divided by $x - 1$.

$P(1) = 1 + k - 4 + 5 = k + 2$. Set $k + 2 = 8$, so $k = 6$.

**Two unknowns.** You need two pieces of information, which give two equations. Solve them as a linear system (elimination or substitution).

For $P(x) = x^3 + mx^2 + nx - 6$: remainder $-6$ when divided by $x - 1$, remainder $0$ when divided by $x + 2$.

* $P(1) = 1 + m + n - 6 = -6 \;\Rightarrow\; m + n = -1$
* $P(-2) = -8 + 4m - 2n - 6 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; 4m - 2n = 14 \;\Rightarrow\; 2m - n = 7$

Add the two equations: $3m = 6$, so $m = 2$, and then $n = -1 - 2 = -3$.

**Check:** $P(x) = x^3 + 2x^2 - 3x - 6$; $P(1) = 1 + 2 - 3 - 6 = -6$ ✓ and $P(-2) = -8 + 8 + 6 - 6 = 0$ ✓. Always substitute back to check.

**Same remainder for two divisors.** If $P(x)$ leaves the same remainder when divided by $x - p$ and by $x - q$, then $P(p) = P(q)$. Set the two expressions equal and solve.

lessons.title: Applications: dimensions from a volume
lessons.body:
Many measurement problems are polynomial division in disguise.

For a rectangular box, $V = lwh$. If you know the volume $V(x)$ and one dimension, divide to get the product of the other two:

$$\text{area of base} = lw = \frac{V(x)}{h}$$

**Example:** $V(x) = x^3 + 7x^2 + 14x + 8$ and the height is $h = x + 2$.

Dividing gives $\dfrac{x^3 + 7x^2 + 14x + 8}{x + 2} = x^2 + 5x + 4$ with remainder $0$.

Factor the base area: $x^2 + 5x + 4 = (x + 1)(x + 4)$. So possible dimensions are $(x + 1)$ cm by $(x + 4)$ cm by $(x + 2)$ cm.

When $x = 3$: $4$ cm by $7$ cm by $5$ cm, and $V = 140$ cm³. Check: $V(3) = 27 + 63 + 42 + 8 = 140$ ✓

> A remainder of $0$ means the divisor divides **evenly** – it is a factor. You will use this idea constantly in Section 2.2.

keyTerms.definition: The polynomial you divide by; in this chapter a binomial such as $x - b$ or $ax - b$.
The result of the division, $Q(x)$. Its degree is one less than the degree of $P(x)$ when the divisor is linear.
What is left over after division, $R$. When dividing by a linear binomial, the remainder is a constant.
$P(x) = (x - b)Q(x) + R$ — the equation used to check a division.
$\dfrac{P(x)}{x - b} = Q(x) + \dfrac{R}{x - b}$, written with its restriction $x \neq b$.
A value the variable cannot take because it makes the divisor zero.
A term with coefficient $0$ (e.g. $0x^2$) inserted for a missing power so the columns line up.
When $P(x)$ is divided by $x - b$ the remainder is $P(b)$; when divided by $ax - b$ it is $P\left(\frac{b}{a}\right)$.

workedExamples.title: Long division with a remainder
workedExamples.problem: Divide $x^3 + 3x^2 - 5x + 4$ by $x - 1$. Write the result in quotient form, state the restriction and check.
steps: **Divide:** $x^3 \div x = x^2$. **Multiply:** $x^2(x - 1) = x^3 - x^2$. **Subtract:** $(x^3 + 3x^2) - (x^3 - x^2) = 4x^2$. Bring down $-5x$.

workedExamples.title: Remainder theorem with ax − b
workedExamples.problem: Find the remainder when $P(x) = 4x^3 - 6x^2 + 2x - 1$ is divided by $2x - 1$.
steps: Set the divisor to zero: $2x - 1 = 0 \Rightarrow x = \tfrac12$.

workedExamples.title: Solving for an unknown coefficient
workedExamples.problem: Determine $k$ so that $P(x) = 2x^3 + kx^2 - 3x + 4$ leaves a remainder of $10$ when divided by $x + 2$.
steps: By the remainder theorem the remainder is $P(-2)$.

workedExamples.title: Dimensions of a box
workedExamples.problem: The volume of a box is $V(x) = 2x^3 + 7x^2 + 2x - 3$ and the height is $x + 1$. Find expressions for the length and width, and the dimensions when $x = 2$ (units in metres).
steps: Dimensions: $(2x - 1)$ by $(x + 3)$ by $(x + 1)$. When $x = 2$: $3$ m by $5$ m by $3$ m, volume $45$ m³. Check $V(2) = 16 + 28 + 4 - 3 = 45$ ✓

misconceptions.myth: To find the remainder when dividing by $x + 3$, substitute $x = 3$.
You can skip a missing power when dividing, e.g. divide $x^3 - 7x + 6$ as written.
misconceptions.fact: Insert a placeholder $0x^2$ first so like terms stay lined up.
The remainder must also be divided by the divisor: $Q(x) + \dfrac{R}{x - 2}$, with $x \neq 2$.

misconceptions.myth: For a divisor $2x - 1$ the remainder is $P(1)$.
misconceptions.fact: Set $2x - 1 = 0$, so $x = \tfrac12$ and the remainder is $P\left(\tfrac12\right)$.

misconceptions.myth: The remainder theorem gives the quotient too.
misconceptions.fact: It gives only the remainder. Use long (or synthetic) division when you need the quotient.

misconceptions.myth: When subtracting in long division, only the first term changes sign.
misconceptions.fact: Subtract the **whole** line: change the sign of every term, then add.

realWorld.title: Packaging and design
realWorld.body: Engineers model the volume of a container with a polynomial. Dividing by a known dimension (like a fixed height) gives an expression for the base area, which tells them what length and width are possible.

realWorld.title: Checking your own work
realWorld.body: The division statement $P(x) = (x - b)Q(x) + R$ is a built-in error check — the same idea as checking $579 \div 8$ by computing $8 \times 72 + 3$.

realWorld.title: Quick evaluation
realWorld.body: The remainder theorem says dividing by $x - b$ and evaluating $P(b)$ give the same number. That shortcut lets you evaluate a polynomial or test a value quickly, which is how calculators and computers evaluate polynomials efficiently.

realWorld.title: Error-detecting codes
realWorld.body: Computers detect transmission errors in data (such as Wi-Fi packets) by treating the data as a polynomial and checking the remainder after dividing by an agreed polynomial. A nonzero remainder signals an error.

practice.question: Divide $x^3 + 2x^2 - 5x - 6$ by $x - 2$. What does the remainder tell you?
practice.hint: Use Divide → Multiply → Subtract → Bring down three times.
practice.solution: Quotient $x^2 + 4x + 3$, remainder $0$. Check: $P(2) = 8 + 8 - 10 - 6 = 0$. A remainder of $0$ means $x - 2$ divides evenly, so it is a factor: $x^3 + 2x^2 - 5x - 6 = (x - 2)(x + 1)(x + 3)$.

practice.question: Find the remainder when $P(x) = x^4 - 3x^2 + 2x - 5$ is divided by $x + 1$.
Divide $3x^3 - 4x + 2$ by $x - 1$ and write the division statement.
What is the remainder when $P(x) = 6x^3 + x^2 - 4x + 3$ is divided by $3x + 1$?
Find $k$ if $x^3 - kx^2 + 2x + 1$ has remainder $-3$ when divided by $x - 2$.
practice.hint: Write $P(2)$ in terms of $k$ and set it equal to $-3$.

practice.question: Explain why the remainder after dividing by $x - 5$ cannot contain an $x$ term.
practice.hint: Compare the degree of the remainder with the degree of the divisor.
practice.solution: You keep dividing while the remainder's degree is at least the divisor's degree. The divisor has degree 1, so you stop only when the remainder has degree 0 — a constant.

practice.question: The volume of a box is $V(x) = x^3 + 6x^2 + 11x + 6$ and the height is $x + 3$. Find the possible length and width.
For what value of $b$ does $P(x) = x^3 + bx - 4$ leave the same remainder when divided by $x - 1$ and by $x + 1$?

summary: Long division of polynomials repeats **divide, multiply, subtract, bring down**; use placeholders for missing terms.
Division statement: $P(x) = (x - b)Q(x) + R$. Quotient form: $\frac{P(x)}{x - b} = Q(x) + \frac{R}{x - b}$, $x \neq b$.
Check a division with divisor × quotient + remainder = dividend.
**Remainder theorem:** dividing $P(x)$ by $x - b$ leaves remainder $P(b)$; dividing by $ax - b$ leaves $P\left(\frac{b}{a}\right)$.
Knowing a remainder gives an equation, so you can solve for unknown coefficients.

questions.text: Use the remainder theorem to determine the remainder when $P(x) = x^3 + {{a}}x^2 - {{b}}x + {{c}}$ is divided by $x - {{k}}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the remainder.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Is $x - {{k}}$ a factor of $P(x)$? Explain how you know.

questions.modelAnswer:
Set the divisor equal to zero: $x - {{k}} = 0$, so $x = {{k}}$.

$P({{k}}) = ({{k}})^3 + {{a}}({{k}})^2 - {{b}}({{k}}) + {{c}}$

$= {{k^3}} + {{a*k^2}} - {{b*k}} + {{c}}$

$= {{R}}$

(b) Since the remainder is ${{R}}$, not $0$, the binomial $x - {{k}}$ does not divide evenly into $P(x)$, so it is **not** a factor. (If the remainder had been $0$, it would be a factor.)

rubric.point: Identifies that the remainder is $P(k)$ (substitutes the correct value)
Substitutes and evaluates each term correctly
Explains that a nonzero remainder means it is not a factor

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the result in quotient form.

parts.label: b

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the corresponding division statement and use it (or the remainder theorem) to check your answer.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Long division**

1. $x^3 \div x = x^2$. $x^2(x - {{k}}) = x^3 - {{k}}x^2$. Subtract: $({{a}} + {{k}})x^2 = {{q1}}x^2$. Bring down ${{b}}x$.
2. ${{q1}}x^2 \div x = {{q1}}x$. ${{q1}}x(x - {{k}}) = {{q1}}x^2 - {{q1*k}}x$. Subtract: $({{b}} + {{q1*k}})x = {{q0}}x$. Bring down ${{c}}$.
3. ${{q0}}x \div x = {{q0}}$. ${{q0}}(x - {{k}}) = {{q0}}x - {{q0*k}}$. Subtract: ${{c}} + {{q0*k}} = {{R}}$.

Quotient: $x^2 + {{q1}}x + {{q0}}$, remainder ${{R}}$.

(a) $\dfrac{x^3 + {{a}}x^2 + {{b}}x + {{c}}}{x - {{k}}} = x^2 + {{q1}}x + {{q0}} + \dfrac{ {{R}} }{x - {{k}}}$

(b) Restriction: $x \neq {{k}}$, because the divisor $x - {{k}}$ would be $0$ and division by zero is undefined.

(c) $x^3 + {{a}}x^2 + {{b}}x + {{c}} = (x - {{k}})(x^2 + {{q1}}x + {{q0}}) + {{R}}$.
Check with the remainder theorem: $P({{k}}) = {{k^3}} + {{a*k^2}} + {{b*k}} + {{c}} = {{R}}$ ✓

rubric.point: Correct first quotient term and subtraction
Correct second and third quotient terms
Quotient form written correctly (remainder over divisor)
Division statement and a valid check

questions.text: Divide $x^3 - {{a}}x + {{c}}$ by $x - {{k}}$. Explain why a placeholder is needed and write the result in quotient form.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is the remainder?

questions.modelAnswer:
The dividend has no $x^2$ term, so write it as $x^3 + 0x^2 - {{a}}x + {{c}}$. The placeholder keeps the $x^2$, $x$ and constant columns lined up so like terms are subtracted from like terms.

1. $x^3 \div x = x^2$; $x^2(x - {{k}}) = x^3 - {{k}}x^2$; subtract: $0x^2 - (-{{k}}x^2) = {{k}}x^2$. Bring down $-{{a}}x$.
2. ${{k}}x^2 \div x = {{k}}x$; ${{k}}x(x - {{k}}) = {{k}}x^2 - {{k^2}}x$; subtract: $-{{a}}x + {{k^2}}x = {{q0}}x$. Bring down ${{c}}$.
3. ${{q0}}x \div x = {{q0}}$; ${{q0}}(x - {{k}}) = {{q0}}x - {{q0*k}}$; subtract: ${{c}} + {{q0*k}} = {{R}}$.

$$\frac{x^3 - {{a}}x + {{c}}}{x - {{k}}} = x^2 + {{k}}x + {{q0}} + \frac{ {{R}} }{x - {{k}}},\quad x \neq {{k}}$$

Check: $P({{k}}) = {{k^3}} - {{a*k}} + {{c}} = {{R}}$ ✓

rubric.point: Explains the need for the $0x^2$ placeholder
Sets up the division with the placeholder

questions.text: Divide $6x^3 + {{p2}}x^2 + {{p1}}x + {{p0}}$ by $2x - 1$. Write the result in quotient form and state the restriction. Then verify the remainder using the remainder theorem.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the remainder.

questions.modelAnswer:
1. $6x^3 \div 2x = 3x^2$; $3x^2(2x - 1) = 6x^3 - 3x^2$; subtract: ${{p2}}x^2 + 3x^2 = {{2*a}}x^2$. Bring down ${{p1}}x$.
2. ${{2*a}}x^2 \div 2x = {{a}}x$; ${{a}}x(2x - 1) = {{2*a}}x^2 - {{a}}x$; subtract: ${{p1}}x + {{a}}x = {{2*b}}x$. Bring down ${{p0}}$.
3. ${{2*b}}x \div 2x = {{b}}$; ${{b}}(2x - 1) = {{2*b}}x - {{b}}$; subtract: ${{p0}} + {{b}} = {{r}}$.

$$\frac{6x^3 + {{p2}}x^2 + {{p1}}x + {{p0}}}{2x - 1} = 3x^2 + {{a}}x + {{b}} + \frac{ {{r}} }{2x - 1},\quad x \neq \tfrac12$$

**Verify:** the divisor is zero when $x = \tfrac12$.
$P\left(\tfrac12\right) = 6\left(\tfrac18\right) + {{p2}}\left(\tfrac14\right) + {{p1}}\left(\tfrac12\right) + {{p0}} = {{0.75 + p2/4 + p1/2 + p0:4}}$ ✓ equals the remainder.

questions.text: The volume, in cubic centimetres, of a rectangular box is $V(x) = x^3 + {{s1}}x^2 + {{s2}}x + {{s3}}$. The height of the box is $x + {{p}}$ centimetres.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine an expression for the area of the base.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine expressions for the possible length and width.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the dimensions and the volume of the box when $x = {{X}}$.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Base area $= \dfrac{V(x)}{h} = \dfrac{x^3 + {{s1}}x^2 + {{s2}}x + {{s3}}}{x + {{p}}}$.

Long division: $x^3 \div x = x^2$; $x^2(x + {{p}}) = x^3 + {{p}}x^2$; subtract → ${{q+r}}x^2 + {{s2}}x$.
${{q+r}}x^2 \div x = {{q+r}}x$; ${{q+r}}x(x + {{p}}) = {{q+r}}x^2 + {{p*(q+r)}}x$; subtract → ${{q*r}}x + {{s3}}$.
${{q*r}}x \div x = {{q*r}}$; ${{q*r}}(x + {{p}}) = {{q*r}}x + {{q*r*p}}$; remainder $0$.

Base area $= x^2 + {{q+r}}x + {{q*r}}$.

(b) Factor: two numbers that multiply to ${{q*r}}$ and add to ${{q+r}}$ are ${{q}}$ and ${{r}}$, so $x^2 + {{q+r}}x + {{q*r}} = (x + {{q}})(x + {{r}})$. Possible dimensions: $(x + {{q}})$ cm by $(x + {{r}})$ cm by $(x + {{p}})$ cm.

(c) When $x = {{X}}$: ${{X+q}}$ cm by ${{X+r}}$ cm by ${{X+p}}$ cm. Volume $= {{X+q}} \times {{X+r}} \times {{X+p}} = {{(X+q)*(X+r)*(X+p)}}$ cm³.
Check: $V({{X}}) = {{X^3}} + {{s1*X^2}} + {{s2*X}} + {{s3}} = {{(X+q)*(X+r)*(X+p)}}$ ✓

rubric.point: Recognises that base area = volume ÷ height
Divides correctly to get the base area
States all three dimensions in terms of $x$

questions.text: Explain, using the division statement $P(x) = (x - b)Q(x) + R$, why the remainder when $P(x)$ is divided by $x - b$ is $P(b)$. Then explain what the remainder tells you about the graph of $y = P(x)$.
questions.modelAnswer:
The division statement is true for every value of $x$. Substituting $x = b$:

$P(b) = (b - b)Q(b) + R = 0 \cdot Q(b) + R = R$.

The factor $(x - b)$ becomes zero, wiping out the quotient term, so only the remainder is left. That is the remainder theorem.

**Graph:** $P(b) = R$ means the point $(b, R)$ lies on the graph of $y = P(x)$. The remainder is the $y$-value (height) of the graph at $x = b$. If $R = 0$, the graph crosses or touches the $x$-axis at $x = b$.

rubric.point: Substitutes $x = b$ into the division statement
Connects the remainder to the point $(b, R)$ on the graph

questions.text:
A student wrote:

$$\frac{x^3 - 2x^2 + 4x - 5}{x - 1} = x^2 - x + 3 - 2$$

Identify the error(s), write the correct result, and verify it.
questions.modelAnswer:
Errors:
1. The remainder $-2$ must be divided by the divisor. It should be $\dfrac{-2}{x - 1}$, not $-2$.
2. The restriction $x \neq 1$ is missing.

Correct: $\dfrac{x^3 - 2x^2 + 4x - 5}{x - 1} = x^2 - x + 3 - \dfrac{2}{x - 1},\ x \neq 1$.

Verify with the division statement: $(x - 1)(x^2 - x + 3) - 2 = x^3 - x^2 + 3x - x^2 + x - 3 - 2 = x^3 - 2x^2 + 4x - 5$ ✓.
Or with the remainder theorem: $P(1) = 1 - 2 + 4 - 5 = -2$ ✓.

rubric.point: Identifies that the remainder must be written over the divisor
Verifies by multiplying back or by the remainder theorem

questions.text: A student says the remainder when $P(x) = 4x^3 + 2x^2 - 6x + 5$ is divided by $2x + 1$ is $P(1)$. Explain the mistake and find the correct remainder.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the correct remainder.

questions.modelAnswer:
The value to substitute is the one that makes the divisor zero: $2x + 1 = 0 \Rightarrow x = -\tfrac12$. Substituting $x = 1$ would only give the remainder for the divisor $x - 1$.

$P\left(-\tfrac12\right) = 4\left(-\tfrac18\right) + 2\left(\tfrac14\right) - 6\left(-\tfrac12\right) + 5 = -\tfrac12 + \tfrac12 + 3 + 5 = 8$

The remainder is $8$.

rubric.point: Explains that the divisor must be set to zero

questions.text: Create a cubic polynomial $P(x)$ that leaves a remainder of $7$ when divided by $x - 2$. Explain your method, then verify your polynomial in two different ways.
questions.modelAnswer:
**One method:** choose any quadratic quotient, e.g. $Q(x) = x^2 + 1$, and build $P(x)$ from the division statement:

$P(x) = (x - 2)(x^2 + 1) + 7 = x^3 - 2x^2 + x - 2 + 7 = x^3 - 2x^2 + x + 5$

**Verification 1 (remainder theorem):** $P(2) = 8 - 8 + 2 + 5 = 7$ ✓

**Verification 2 (long division):** dividing $x^3 - 2x^2 + x + 5$ by $x - 2$ gives quotient $x^2 + 1$ and remainder $7$ ✓

(Another method: start from any cubic $P(x)$, calculate $P(2)$, and adjust the constant term so that $P(2) = 7$.) Many answers are possible.

rubric.point: Clear explanation of the method (division statement or adjusting the constant)

questions.text: The remainder when $P(x)$ is divided by $x - {{k}}$ is ${{R}}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name one point that must lie on the graph of $y = P(x)$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Does the graph of $y = P(x)$ have an $x$-intercept at $x = {{k}}$? Explain.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why $x - {{k}}$ must be a factor of $P(x) - {{R}}$.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) By the remainder theorem $P({{k}}) = {{R}}$, so the point $({{k}}, {{R}})$ is on the graph of $y = P(x)$.

(b) Not necessarily — a remainder of ${{R}}$ (not zero) means $x - {{k}}$ is **not** a factor. The graph does **not** cross the $x$-axis at $x = {{k}}$; it passes through height ${{R}}$ there.

(c) $P(x) - {{R}}$: dividing by $x - {{k}}$ leaves remainder $P({{k}}) - {{R}} = 0$. So $x - {{k}}$ **is** a factor of $P(x) - {{R}}$.

rubric.point: Explains that a nonzero remainder means not a factor / not an $x$-intercept
Shows that $P(x) - R$ has remainder 0, so $x - k$ is a factor

questions.text: Let $f(x) = x^4 + kx^3 - {{a}}x - {{c}}$. When $f(x)$ is divided by $x - {{m}}$, the remainder is ${{R1}}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the value of $k$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the remainder when $f(x)$ is divided by $x + {{m}}$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how you could verify your answer to part (b).

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $f({{m}}) = {{m^4}} + {{m^3}}k - {{a*m}} - {{c}} = {{R1}}$

${{m^3}}k = {{R1 - m^4 + a*m + c}}$, so $k = {{k}}$.

(b) Remainder when divided by $x + {{m}}$ is $f(-{{m}})$:

$f(-{{m}}) = {{m^4}} + ({{k}})(-{{m}})^3 - {{a}}(-{{m}}) - {{c}} = {{m^4}} + {{-k*m^3}} + {{a*m}} - {{c}} = {{R2}}$

(c) You can verify by long division of $x^4 + {{k}}x^3 + 0x^2 - {{a}}x - {{c}}$ by $x + {{m}}$ (placeholder needed for $x^2$) or by graphing $y = f(x)$ and reading the $y$-value at $x = -{{m}}$, which should be ${{R2}}$.

questions.text: Explain the difference between the dividend, divisor, quotient and remainder using both a numerical example and a polynomial example. Why is the remainder after dividing a polynomial by a linear binomial always a constant?
questions.modelAnswer:
**Numerical:** $23 \div 5$: dividend $23$, divisor $5$, quotient $4$, remainder $3$, because $23 = 5 \times 4 + 3$.

**Polynomial:** $(x^2 + 3x + 5) \div (x + 1)$: dividend $x^2 + 3x + 5$, divisor $x + 1$, quotient $x + 2$, remainder $3$, because $(x + 1)(x + 2) + 3 = x^2 + 3x + 5$.

The remainder must have a **lower degree than the divisor** — otherwise you could keep dividing. A linear divisor has degree 1, so the remainder has degree 0, which means it is a constant.

rubric.point: Correct numerical example with all four parts
Correct polynomial example with all four parts
Explains why the remainder's degree is less than the divisor's degree
